subject: Science
title: Year 9 Science Exam 4
topic: Biology · Inheritance, variation and evolution · AQA Higher
intro: You may use a calculator. For longer answers write in full sentences and use key words. Describe = say what happens; Explain = say what happens and why (use because and so); Compare = similarities and differences (use whereas); Evaluate = points for and against, then a justified conclusion. 6-mark questions are marked on how well your ideas link together: plan for a minute, then write about 6 linked points.

questions.q: What is an allele?
options: A section of DNA found on every chromosome
A different form of the same gene
A thread-like structure found in the nucleus
The full set of genes in an organism
questions.ms: B1: a different form (version) of the same gene.

questions.q: A person has the alleles Hh for a characteristic. Which word describes this genotype?
questions.ms: B1: heterozygous (two different alleles).

questions.q: Which of these is an example of discontinuous variation?
questions.ms: B1: blood group. It falls into separate groups (A, B, AB, O) with nothing in between.

questions.q: Which of these is a biotic factor?
questions.ms: B1: number of predators. Biotic factors are living; the others are abiotic (non-living).

questions.q: Which type of reproduction produces offspring that are genetically identical to the parent?
questions.ms: B1: asexual reproduction (one parent, no mixing of genes).

questions.q:
In rabbits, the allele for brown fur (B) is dominant over the allele for white fur (b).
Two brown rabbits have some white babies. Explain how this is possible.
questions.ms: B1: both parents must be heterozygous / carriers (Bb). B1: each parent passes on the recessive allele b, so the white babies are bb.

questions.q:
A heterozygous brown rabbit (Bb) mates with a white rabbit (bb).
Use a Punnett square for this cross. Type the gametes of each parent and the genotypes of the four offspring.
questions.ms: B1: gametes B and b from the brown parent, b and b from the white parent. B1: offspring Bb, Bb, bb, bb. B1: phenotypes linked correctly (Bb = brown, bb = white).

questions.q: What percentage of the offspring would you expect to have white fur? (%)
questions.ms: Answer: 50%. B1 (2 out of 4 offspring are bb).

questions.q:
The rabbits in 6(b) have a litter of 8 babies: 6 are brown and 2 are white.
Explain why this is different from the expected ratio.
questions.ms: B1: the ratio is only a probability / fertilisation is random (which sperm meets which egg is chance). B1: with a small number of offspring, results are less likely to match the expected ratio; a larger number would get closer to 1 : 1.

questions.q:
Ali and Omar are identical twins. Ali grew up in Dubai and Omar grew up in London.
As adults they have the same eye colour and the same blood group, but Ali has darker skin and Omar is 6 kg heavier.
Explain these similarities and differences.
questions.ms: B1: identical twins have the same genes / DNA (from one fertilised egg). B1: eye colour and blood group are inherited / controlled by genes only, so they are the same. B1: skin colour and body mass are also affected by the environment. B1: a specific link, e.g. more sun in Dubai darkens skin; different diet or exercise changes mass.

questions.q:
The Arabian sand gazelle lives in the deserts of the UAE. It has pale, sandy-coloured fur. Scientists think its ancestors had darker fur.
Explain how natural selection could have led to the sand gazelle having pale fur.
questions.ms: 6 marks, level-marked. Level 3 (5-6 marks): a detailed, logically linked answer covering most points. Level 2 (3-4 marks): several relevant points, some linked. Level 1 (1-2 marks): simple, separate statements. Indicative content: there was variation in fur colour in the population; caused by mutations / different alleles; predators (e.g. wolves, caracals) could see darker gazelles more easily on pale sand; pale gazelles were camouflaged, so were less likely to be eaten and more likely to survive; survivors reproduced; passed on the alleles for pale fur to their offspring; over many generations the allele for pale fur became more common, so most of the population now has pale fur.

questions.q: Explain why doctors should not give antibiotics to people who have a cold.
questions.ms: B1: colds are caused by viruses. B1: antibiotics only kill bacteria / do not work on viruses. B1: overusing antibiotics increases the chance of antibiotic-resistant bacteria developing (resistant bacteria survive and reproduce).

questions.q:
Emperor penguins live in Antarctica, where it is very cold and windy.
Give one structural, one behavioural and one functional adaptation of emperor penguins, and explain how each one helps them survive.
questions.ms: B1 structural, e.g. thick layer of fat (blubber) / dense waterproof feathers, insulates the body. B1 behavioural, e.g. huddling in large groups, reduces heat loss from each penguin / taking turns in the middle. B1 functional, e.g. slowing their metabolism or heart rate to save energy / special blood vessels in the feet that reduce heat loss. Each mark needs the adaptation and how it helps.

questions.q:
A student uses a transect and quadrats to study how the number of dandelions changes with distance from a large tree. Her results and light readings are in the table below.
Distance from tree (m)02468
Light intensity (units)150320480630700
Trial 1147910
Trial 22381511
Trial 30561012

Name the independent variable in her investigation.
questions.ms: B1: distance from the tree.

questions.q: Which of these is a control variable in her investigation?
questions.ms: B1: size of the quadrat (kept the same each time to make it a fair test).

questions.q: One result in the table is anomalous. Write down the anomalous value.
questions.ms: Answer: 15 (Trial 2 at 6 m). B1: it is much higher than the other two results at 6 m (9 and 10).

questions.q: Calculate the mean number of dandelions at 6 m. Do not include the anomalous result.
questions.ms: Answer: 9.5. M1 for (9 + 10) ÷ 2. A1 for 9.5.

questions.q: Describe the relationship between distance from the tree and the number of dandelions. Use the light intensity data to explain it.
questions.ms: B1: as distance from the tree increases, the number of dandelions increases (e.g. mean of 1 at 0 m, 11 at 8 m). B1: light intensity also increases with distance, because the tree's leaves cause shade. B1: more light means more photosynthesis, so more dandelions can grow / survive.

questions.q: Which type of graph should she draw to show how the mean number of dandelions changes with distance?
questions.ms: B1: line graph, because both distance and number of dandelions are continuous (numerical) data.

questions.q: Suggest two ways she could make her results more repeatable or more valid.
questions.ms: B1 each for any two: repeat the transect in other places / around other trees; use more quadrats at each distance; place quadrats at the same time of day; use a light meter at every quadrat; count the same way every time (e.g. a plant counts if more than half is inside).

questions.q: Give two factors that may cause a species to become extinct.
questions.ms: B1 each for any two: new predators; new diseases; new competitors; changes to the environment / climate change; habitat destruction; hunting.

questions.q:
The Arabian leopard is critically endangered. Only a few hundred are left in the wild.
Describe and explain two ways people could help to stop the Arabian leopard becoming extinct.
questions.ms: For each of two ways: B1 the method and B1 the explanation. E.g. captive breeding programmes, so numbers increase and animals can be released into the wild; protecting its habitat / nature reserves, so it has space, shelter and prey; banning hunting, so fewer are killed; protecting its prey animals, so it has enough food; gene banks (storing sperm/eggs), so genetic variety is kept for the future.

questions.q:
A lion and a tiger can mate in a zoo. Their offspring is called a liger. Ligers are usually infertile.
Explain why lions and tigers are classed as different species.
questions.ms: B1: a species is a group of organisms that can mate to produce fertile offspring. B1: ligers are infertile (cannot reproduce), so lions and tigers are different species.

questions.q:
A farmer grows a field of banana plants. All the plants were grown asexually from one parent plant.
A new disease arrives. Explain why the disease could kill all of the banana plants.
questions.ms: B1: asexual reproduction produces clones / genetically identical plants. B1: there is no variation in the population. B1: so if one plant is not resistant to the disease, none are resistant / no plants have alleles to survive it. (Contrast with sexual reproduction, which produces variation, may be credited.)

questions.q:
Grey squirrels were brought to the UK from North America. Since then the number of native red squirrels has fallen a lot.
Suggest and explain why the number of red squirrels has fallen. Use the idea of competition in your answer.
questions.ms: B1: grey and red squirrels compete for the same resources, e.g. food (nuts, seeds), space / territory, nesting sites. B1: grey squirrels are bigger / better competitors, so they get more of the resources. B1: red squirrels get less food / shelter, so fewer survive and reproduce. B1: grey squirrels may also carry a disease (squirrel pox) that kills red squirrels / any other valid linked point.
